title.purpose: SwiftUI .title2 bold: event name in the detail, headline of the access screen. .title3 for the editor's title field (semibold) and the agenda's day number (bold).

headline.purpose: SwiftUI .headline: month name above the month navigator.

body.purpose: SwiftUI .body: event titles in the day sheet and agenda, form rows, sidebar calendar names.

day-number.purpose: SwiftUI .callout semibold with tabular figures; .footnote in columns under 130 pt. Day numbers in the month and in time-grid headers.

detail.purpose: SwiftUI .subheadline: date and time under a detail title, supporting line of a day-sheet row. Also the month event row on Mac.

event-row.purpose: SwiftUI .caption; .caption2 and condensed width in columns under 130 pt. Time and title of an event in a month cell.

label.purpose: SwiftUI .caption semibold: weekday header, event block titles, section labels inside the detail. Sentence case.

micro.purpose: SwiftUI .caption2 with tabular figures: hour labels, time and place inside a block. Semibold for the label set into a span line.

narrative.overview:
Daybook draws a month the way a network map draws a city. Each calendar is a line in its own colour, each event is a station dot on that line, an event that lasts several days is a horizontal line with rounded ends, and today is the interchange circle. The ground is one flat colour, midnight blue in the dark appearance and porcelain in the light one, and the two swap roles as ink. There is no third brand colour: every other colour on screen belongs to a calendar and was chosen by the user.

The system is dense and quiet. Week rows take the height of their fullest day, so the grid is uneven on purpose and no day ends in a count of hidden events. Type is the system face at Dynamic Type text styles with tabular figures, condensed when a column gets narrow. Structure comes from hairlines at low opacity and one step of tonal depth between the ground and the rail; controls, sheets and bars are the platform's own.

This record describes the SwiftUI build for iOS 26 and macOS 26. Sizes are points at the default text size and scale with Dynamic Type. Values in the frontmatter with a `-dark` or `-light` suffix are the two appearances of one adaptive token; `midnight` and `porcelain` are ground in one appearance and ink in the other.
keyCharacteristics: Two grounds, one ink each, swapped between appearances; no brand accent.
Calendar colour appears only as line: a 3 pt vertical segment, an 8 pt horizontal line, a 22% tint of a block.
Every event is on screen; rows grow, cells never collapse into a count.
System type, tabular figures, condensed width under 130 pt columns.
Hairlines and one tonal step instead of shadows and cards.

rules.name: The Line Is the Only Colour Rule
rules.body: Hue on a calendar surface means "this calendar" and nothing else. Interface state, selection and emphasis are drawn in ink: the selected day is an ink ring, today is an ink circle, the current time is an ink line.

rules.name: The Thinned Line Rule
rules.body: A calendar colour used as a fill is mixed 22% into the ground in OKLab, never laid over it as transparency and never mixed in sRGB. The result is opaque, keeps ink legible on it, and keeps warm colours from turning brown on midnight.

rules.name: The Colour Plus Name Rule
rules.body: A calendar is never identified by colour alone. Wherever a calendar is chosen or named (sidebar, picker rows, event detail, day sheet, VoiceOver labels) its title is beside the colour.

rules.name: The Tabular Figures Rule
rules.body: Every number that sits in a column is set with tabular figures: day numbers, times, hour labels. In a month row the time is right-aligned in a slot as wide as "00:00", so titles share one left edge.

rules.name: The Condense Before You Cut Rule
rules.body: When a column is narrower than 130 pt, type switches to the condensed width and insets tighten before anything is removed. The month row then drops its time; the title stays.

rules.name: The No Broken Words Rule
rules.body: Text in a cell or block never wraps inside a word. Titles hold one line with a tail ellipsis (two lines in blocks 140 pt or wider); a time shows as a range, then as a start, then not at all, whichever fits whole.

rules.name: The Nothing Hidden Rule
rules.body: A day shows every event of its enabled calendars. Rows grow, strips grow, views scroll; no cell ends in "+3 more", a dot, or a count.

rules.name: The Rows Before Columns Rule
rules.body: When columns cannot hold a title at the current text size, the layout changes to full-width rows. It does not shrink type and it does not truncate the list.

rules.name: The One Step Rule
rules.body: There are two surface levels, ground and rail. A new surface is one of them; it does not introduce a third tone, a gradient or a shadow.

dos: Do draw calendar colour only as line: a 3 pt vertical segment, an 8 pt horizontal line, or a 22% OKLab tint of a block.
Do mark selection, today and the current time in ink (ring, filled circle, 2 pt line).
Do put new sheets on the rail colour with their rows in the ground colour.
Do set every figure that aligns in a column with tabular figures.
Do switch to condensed width below 130 pt columns, and to full-width rows at accessibility text sizes.
Do keep a calendar's name next to its colour wherever a calendar is identified.
Do check any new text colour on a tinted block against 4.5:1 in both appearances, and any new preset line colour against 3:1 on both grounds.
Do build new metrics as scaled metrics tied to a text style, so they grow with Dynamic Type.
donts: Don't hide events behind a count, a dot or a "more" link in any view.
Don't give the interface a hue of its own on a calendar surface; a coloured control reads as a calendar line.
Don't fill a block or a row with a calendar colour at full strength, or thin it with opacity instead of the OKLab mix.
Don't add shadows, gradients or a third surface tone.
Don't round the end of a span line where the event continues into another week.
Don't let text break inside a word; truncate the title, then drop the time.
Don't replace the navigator, the station mark or the interchange circle with system pickers or badges that bring their own accent colour.
